# Use skill-author

<!-- Generated by build_pack_guides.py from pack.json and the skills' own files. Edit those, not this. -->

Write a new portable Agent Skill (a SKILL.md folder) from a described task, for Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Kiro or Antigravity in any repo — a description that leads with the artifact and ends with trigger phrases, decisive steps, a quality bar, when and when-not sections naming near-miss siblings, anti-patterns, a non-interactive rule, reference files and scripts that work in every tool, acceptance evals and trigger queries, and the install path for each tool.

**Reach for it when** the user says "turn this into a skill", "write a SKILL.md for…", "make an agent skill that…", or wants a repeatable task packaged so their coding agent does it the same way every time.

## Install it

```bash
npx skilldrop-cli install skill-author                 # Claude Code, your user folder
npx skilldrop-cli install skill-author --project       # Claude Code, this repo
npx skilldrop-cli install skill-author --ide cursor    # or kiro, codex, antigravity, copilot
```

It is part of the Skill engineering pack: [`--pack skill-engineering`](../packs/use-the-skill-engineering-pack.md) installs it with its neighbours.

## Ask for it

Say it the way you would to a colleague. Requests like these route to it:

- "Turn this prompt I keep pasting into a reusable skill for Claude Code"
- "Write a SKILL.md that makes our agent draft API changelogs the same way every time"
- "Make an agent skill that converts our Jira export into a sprint summary, it has to work in Copilot and Cursor"
- "Help me package our code-review checklist as a skill for Codex"

Requests like these belong to a different skill, so it shouldn't answer them:

- "Add a new skill to the skilldrop catalogue with its manifest and catalogue row"
- "Review my existing skill folder and tell me if it's ready to publish"
- "Generate eval cases for the SKILL.md I already have"

If another skill answers instead, ask for this one by name: "use skill-author".

## Check what you get

A good result:

- **The description leads with the artifact and ends with trigger phrases** a user would actually type, and is under 1,024 characters.
- **Name equals folder name**, kebab-case, at most 64 characters.
- **Every near-miss sibling the user named appears twice:** in a When NOT line and in a should-not-trigger query.
- **Steps decide.** No "consider", "you might", or "depending on preference"; at most two clarifying questions.
- **A quality bar and anti-patterns are present**, and the evals' assertions restate the quality bar as checkable claims.
- **Portable:** every script appears in both the `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` form and the plain relative form; no absolute paths; no tool-only syntax without saying what other tools do.
- **Nothing is invented.** Install paths come from the reference table, and example outputs come from real runs.

## Use something else when

- Adding a skill to the skilldrop catalogue itself, with its manifest, pack and `validate.py` rules: follow that repo's `AGENTS.md` and run `python3 validate.py`
- Auditing a skill that already exists: use `skill-review`
- Adding evals to an existing skill without changing it: use `eval-harness-generator`
- Repo-wide always-on rules for agents (commands, conventions, forbidden actions): use `agents-md-generator`
